items.title: We’re launching Humanity’s First Exam and a Kaggle hackathon to test LLM reliability.
items.summary: Google launches Humanity’s First Exam to test LLM reliability across 544 prompts.
items.body:
We’re launching Humanity’s First Exam and a Kaggle hackathon to test LLM reliability.

Oran Kelly

Research Scientist, Google DeepMind

Nov 24, 2026

Today, we’re launching the Humanity’s First Exam (HFE) benchmark on Kaggle to measure how reliably LLMs answer straightforward, everyday questions. Current frontier models excel at complex math, coding, and science, with most benchmarks measuring these domain-specific capability ceilings.

Instead of focusing on whether a model is capable of solving a task once, HFE measures whether models can consistently solve tasks (and slight variations) every single time. The dataset consists of 544 elementary text and image prompts across 20 foundational capabilities. Over the last 6 months, frontier models have made significant progress on HFE.

Explore the live leaderboard, or read our technical report.

To keep the HFE benchmark dataset up to date, we’re inviting the community to help. Join our three-week Kaggle competition through December 15 and submit everyday questions that today’s models still get wrong.

Example prompt from Humanity’s First Exam’s public dataset: “List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon.” (Answer: green; yellow; white; blue; blue)

items.summary: Google Gemini partners with Golden State to power fan experiences and business operations for the Warriors, Valkyries, and Chase Center. See the news.
items.body:
How Gemini is changing the game for Golden State's organization and fans.

Nov 24, 2026

Today, we’re expanding our partnership with Golden State — making Google Gemini the Official AI Assistant Partner and Official Generative AI & Enterprise LLM Partner of the Warriors, the 2026 WNBA Champion Valkyries, and Chase Center.

The collaboration integrates Gemini across the entire franchise ecosystem. For fans, that means a more interactive game-day experience, both inside Chase Center via interactive videoboard features, and across digital channels for fans following from home. And behind the scenes, Golden State is deploying Gemini for business to build custom AI agents, helping their teams work smarter across both business and basketball operations.

As a Founding Partner of Chase Center since 2019, Golden State has used our gen AI tools to help their operations run smoother, and this next chapter brings the best of Gemini to the team and fans alike.

items.summary: 美国联邦通信委员会（FCC）将于 12 月投票，启动针对外国卫星运营商的对等限制程序。按照提案，只要海外对美国供应商设限，美国就会对当地企业实施同等限制。 提案重点反击欧盟 2 GHz 频谱计划，欧盟要求三分之二频谱仅限本土企业，将 SpaceX 和亚马逊 LEO 排除在外。英国因约 75% 航天预算流向欧洲航天局，也可能受限。 The Register 🌸 科技圈· 茶馆 · 投稿
items.body:
美 FCC 12 月表决外国卫星对等限制，反击欧盟频谱新规

美国联邦通信委员会（FCC）将于 12 月投票，启动针对外国卫星运营商的对等限制程序。按照提案，只要海外对美国供应商设限，美国就会对当地企业实施同等限制。

提案重点反击欧盟 2 GHz 频谱计划，欧盟要求三分之二频谱仅限本土企业，将 SpaceX 和亚马逊 LEO 排除在外。英国因约 75% 航天预算流向欧洲航天局，也可能受限。

外交政策：美国官方和媒体如何粉饰以色列的种族灭绝行为

苏茜·汉森在《外交政策》杂志撰文，通过《跨越红线》和《不要说巴勒斯坦》两本新书，探讨拜登政府与西方主流媒体如何利用语言掩盖加沙战争的残酷现实，以及美国的政治体制、外交政策和新闻报道如何共同为以色列的军事行动提供正当性。

《不要说巴勒斯坦》的作者、中东历史学者阿萨尔·拉德，通过分析《纽约时报》、BBC、路透社等媒体的新闻标题，揭示西方媒体如何使用被动语态、委婉措辞和缺乏历史背景的叙事，淡化以色列的责任。例如，将强制驱逐巴勒斯坦人描述为普通的房屋驱逐纠纷，将无差别轰炸称为“定点打击”，将蓄意制造饥饿描述为“人道主义挑战”。

相比之下，西方媒体在报道乌克兰发生的类似暴行时，通常会明确指出俄罗斯或普京的责任。拉德认为，媒体对以色列官方说法的过度依赖，不仅误导了公众，也使美国政府更加难以正视自身政策造成的灾难。

记者阿克巴尔·沙希德·艾哈迈德的《跨越红线》则通过调查报道，揭示拜登政府内部的决策过程。书中披露，拜登的外交政策团队绕过国会监督和正常行政程序，压制政府内部的反对意见，利用法律解释规避对以色列战争罪行的认定，并质疑人道主义机构和情报部门对加沙饥荒的评估。

即使以色列不断破坏停火谈判、扩大军事行动，拜登政府仍然持续提供武器。美国甚至不惜耗费资源修建海上码头和空投食品，却不愿直接向以色列施压，要求开放正常的人道主义援助渠道。

汉森认为，拜登政府的政策失误不仅源于个人政治利益、官僚体系中的群体思维以及对以色列根深蒂固的情感认同，更涉及美国外交政策长期存在的种族偏见。数十年来，美国一直致力于确保以色列拥有中东地区的军事优势，而加沙战争最终暴露了这一战略所付出的人道主义代价。

文章还批评拜登政府前官员在卸任后继续逃避责任，仿佛他们作为世界上最强大国家的决策者，既无法约束内塔尼亚胡，也无法影响拜登本人。

汉森认为，美国和以色列政治体系中形成的共识共同破坏了国际法律秩序，而西方主流媒体长期以来以谨慎、模糊和所谓客观的语言记录这一过程，却未能充分履行新闻业最重要的职责：监督权力，追究掌权者的责任。

items.title: Independent filmmakers in India bring big-screen stories to life with Google Flow.
items.summary: Indian filmmakers use Google Flow to create original short films. Watch five winning stories from the WIF India Filmathon. See the films now.
items.body:
Independent filmmakers in India bring big-screen stories to life with Google Flow.

Prashant Paulose

Global Lead, Envisioning Studio

Nov 24, 2026

Every culture has its own visual language, and new tools are helping more storytellers share theirs with the world. We partnered with Women in Film India (WIF India) to launch the WIF India × Google Flow Filmathon, designed to democratize AI filmmaking and elevate talent beyond traditional production centers across India.

Using Google Flow, our AI creative studio, participants paired their creative visions with AI to build original worlds from scratch. Five finalist short films recently debuted at the International Film Festival of India in Goa, bringing fresh, creative voices from across the country to the festival screen. The winners received their awards from the Hon’ble Chief Minister of Goa Dr. Pramod Sawant.

Click through the carousel below to watch all five short films made with Google Flow and experience a bold new wave of independent storytelling.

Haunted by visions of his late sister, a brother confronts grief and guilt in “Sikkal,” a chilling folk horror by Promita Banerjee, which took first place in the Filmathon.

A stranger digging a mysterious hole sparks wild rumors across a quiet village in “Kuli,” a sharp Tamil black comedy by Syam Manohar, which came in second place.

In “Pedals of Joy,” a heartfelt animation by Nikhil Shinde, an older brother in Mumbai sets out to fulfill a young boy’s dream. This film took third place.

Aswathi Naduthodi’s visual essay “Bombay Mumbai - Vada Pav,” traces a city’s evolution through the everyday lives connected by one of its most popular street foods.

In Srishti Chaudhary’s dialogue-free animation “Nazar,” a schoolgirl confronts the shadow of the unwanted gaze — and reclaims her sense of hope and power.

items.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
items.summary: GPT-6 models design protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code. Lab tests found evidence of binding across five targets.
items.body:
November 24, 2026

SciencePublication

Read the paper(opens in a new window)

• Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.

• An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.

• In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.

• The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.

In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.

Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.

Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.

Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.

Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.

We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

The models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.

With our research partner, Onava⁠(opens in a new window), we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.

Our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.

We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.

To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.

We tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab. Of those, 35 (10.9%) tested positive for binding to their intended target. We found 5 hits for PD-L1 (a protein some cancers use to evade the immune system), 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. The original RFdiffusion study⁠(opens in a new window) reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. Nevertheless, our results provide early evidence that we can turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins that bind to their intended targets in the lab.

We tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design the sequences itself. We gave it three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose new ones. Specialized models helped us choose which proteins to make and test in the lab.

For three targets, we started with computationally predicted structures of confirmed minibinders whose sequences Onava had collected from earlier studies. In our initial lab screens, we saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). The amino acid sequences proposed by GPT‑6.2 also often differed significantly from the original minibinder sequences, with a median of 50% for VEGF-A, 43% for MDM2, and 15% for PD-1.

We also asked GPT‑6.2 to design new sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes it had generated earlier: two targeting PD-L1 and one targeting IL-7Rα. A specialized model, ProteinMPNN, had already supplied one sequence for each shape, and proteins made from those sequences had shown binding in the lab. Of the 107 proteins made from GPT‑6.2’s new sequences, 14 (13.1%) showed binding.

Given an unpublished structure, GPT‑6.2 had come up with two substantially different sequences that both showed signs of binding to the same target. While lab testing remains a critical part of protein design, our goal is to provide powerful models that can shorten each round of design by giving scientists more control and flexibility, and reduce the total number of design-test cycles needed to find a functional protein. Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language, massively accelerating the development of new biotechnologies and new medicines.

items.body:
🤖 Anthropic 与 🤖 OpenAI 员工称未发布模型强到难以保证安全，内部讨论是否应停止发布

Anthropic 和 OpenAI 均持有远超公开版本的未发布模型，但难以确保安全到可发布。知情人士称，两家内部及 AI 研究界正讨论是否停止公开发布、仅内部部署，甚至是否继续训练新模型。

消息人士称，部分最强的内部模型已经出现完全隐藏推理，或是编造一套虚假思考流程糊弄人类监控者的情况。OpenAI 发言人称目前已采用新安全要求，或放慢发布节奏。Anthropic 发言人表示模型留在公司内部不等于它就是安全的，并称近期有新模型为了开展更多安全核查，推迟了预训练进度。

items.title: 小米营收连续第三个季度出现同比下滑
items.summary: 小米集团营收已经连续第三个季度出现同比下滑。当季总收入1072.4亿元，同比下降5.2%，略高于市场预期的1064.4亿元；净利润38.8亿元，低于市场预期的44.9亿元。经调整净利润为49亿元，同比下降56.8%。与此同时，集团毛利率从去年同期的22.9%降至20.2%。利润下滑主要受到多重因素影响：存储等核心器件成本持续上涨，手机业务毛利率受到挤压；AI业务加大投入，汽车业务则面临产品结构调整。成本压力与战略投入叠加，短期盈利能力受到影响。存储涨价持续挤压手机业务利润。第三季度智能手机毛利率为9.2%，同比下降1.9个百分点。 —— 彭博社、华尔街见闻

items.body:
德国大模型Kolibri 1.1开源，推理GPU耗时降至上代三成

德国 AI 公司 Aleph Alpha 发布 Kolibri 1.1，距离上一代发布仅过去 7 周。新版总参数从 780 亿降至 750 亿，每个 Token 仅激活 34.4 亿参数，继续采用 Apache 2.0 协议开源权重。

Kolibri 1.1 引入稀疏注意力机制，每次只选取上下文中最相关的 2048 个 Token 和最近的 128 个 Token 进行注意力计算，降低长文本推理的计算量和显存读取开销。

模型的思考过程也得到优化，完成每项任务所需的输出 Token 平均减少 41%。两项改进共同作用，使官方测算的单任务 GPU 耗时较上一代降低约 71%。

模型综合评分从 66.6 提升至 73.2，超过 GPT-OSS 120B、Mistral Small 4 和 Nemotron 3 Super。不过，即便在自己主打的德语评测中，Kolibri 1.1 也仅获得 74.2 分，仍落后于中国的 Qwen3.8 Flash Next（81.8 分）和 GLM-5.3 Flash（81.4 分）。

items.title: Searching for distant planets with Astra
items.summary: See how two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to find potential exoplanets in public data from NASA’s Kepler and TESS space telescopes.
items.body:
November 24, 2026

Science

Two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to look for signs of planets in public telescope data. Now they’ve given professional astronomers a few places to look more closely.

Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system⁠(opens in a new window) since the first ones were announced in 1992⁠(opens in a new window). A worldwide community of amateur astronomers has long been part of that search. Some comb through public telescope data for small, repeated dips in a star’s brightness that could signal an orbiting planet. Others use their own telescopes to watch for the next dip and share what they see with researchers.

Astronomers have used AI in this search for years. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope⁠(opens in a new window) that astronomers had already examined. From those examples, the model learned to recognize which patterns in starlight were most likely to come from a planet. When the researchers used it to examine weaker signals, one led them to an eighth planet orbiting a star called Kepler-90⁠(opens in a new window).

Now, tools like Astra are helping amateur astronomers design and run searches of their own, often on data that has already yielded the more obvious exoplanet signals. Kevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, came to astronomy through his love of photographing the night sky. He used Codex to search observations of about 100,000 stars from the Kepler telescope, a planet-hunting mission that ran from 2009 to 2018. Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure start-up Primitive, has always loved astronomy. Working independently of Bond, he tried several AI models before choosing Astra to help him analyze telescope data from about 19 million stars.

Both searches identified potential exoplanets. Bond and Byrd have now turned to astronomers for an independent assessment of their results. Bond contacted an astronomer at the SETI Institute, who ran an independent search and found two of the same signals in the Kepler data. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. It’s in line for further analysis, and two more candidates are awaiting submission.

One of the most common ways to find an exoplanet is to watch the star it orbits. When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view on Earth, it blocks a tiny amount of starlight. Astronomers call that crossing a transit. On a graph of the star’s brightness over time, known as a light curve, a transit shows up as a dip. If the dip keeps coming back at regular intervals, astronomers know when to watch for it again.

Searching for that pattern across thousands of stars is partly a coding problem. Astronomers have published methods for picking out faint, recurring dips in years of measurements. Bond used Codex to compare those methods, combine them in a search program, and test whether changes to the code improved the search. One AI agent scanned the light curves for promising signals. Another ran more detailed checks on the candidates the first one flagged.

Bond ran the program on public data from the Kepler Space Telescope. The search flagged more than 200 signals, including 10 from previously confirmed planets. Finding those known planets gave Bond confidence that the program could pick out the kinds of signals he was looking for.

Two stars stood out. The first, KIC 5689121, is a relatively cool star about half the size of our sun in the constellation Lyra. The Codex search found a dip in brightness every 13.8 days. If a planet is causing it, the amount of light it blocks suggests it could be about 2.4 times Earth’s diameter.

The second star, KIC 6691030, is faint and lies in the northern sky. The Codex search found a dip in its brightness every 4.8 days, consistent with a planet smaller than Neptune. These were the two signals the SETI Institute astronomer found independently. Confirming what caused them could take months or years.

“Kevin’s work shows how citizen scientists, equipped with AI, can help astronomers explore the Kepler Bonus Catalog—a vast collection of stars beyond Kepler’s original targets. His pipeline has surfaced promising candidates in data traditional searches may have missed. Our initial checks are encouraging, and follow-up observations will tell us more.”

Vishal Gajjar, associate director for international SETI programs at the SETI Institute

Byrd used Astra to design two searches. One looked broadly for exoplanet candidates. The other focused on stars’ habitable zones. A habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet with a suitable atmosphere could support liquid water on its surface.

Byrd then asked Astra to review published methods, build the search software, and run initial checks on promising signals. His searches drew on observations from TESS, which NASA launched in 2018, and from other public telescope archives.

The first pass through the data turned up 49 candidates. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on the TESS mission, where it is awaiting further analysis. His search is still running.

When astronomers see a star dim, they have to consider what else might explain it. Two stars passing in front of one another can produce a similar dip. Even a change in temperature aboard a telescope can affect its instruments enough to make a star appear to dim.

Astronomers can use statistics to show that an exoplanet is the most likely explanation for a series of dips. They can also collect more observations, sometimes using a different method. For example, an orbiting planet’s gravity tugs on its star, causing it to move slightly toward and away from us. That motion, called radial velocity, shows up as tiny shifts in the color of the star’s light. Astronomers then publish their findings in a peer-reviewed journal so others can examine the evidence.

For Bond and Byrd, each candidate is a question that can be tested. If a planet is passing in front of the star in Lyra every 13.8 days, astronomers can watch for the next crossing. Further observations can help establish whether the dip repeats as expected, while additional checks can help determine what is causing it.

Photographs by Kevin Bond

You can contribute without owning a telescope. NASA’s Exoplanet Watch⁠(opens in a new window) lets you request data and learn to plot a light curve yourself. Its broader exoplanet citizen science programs⁠(opens in a new window) offer other ways to participate.

If you have access to a telescope, Exoplanet Watch walks users through how to collect data on transiting exoplanets and participate in observation campaigns. AAVSO’s Exoplanet Observing Program⁠(opens in a new window) can show you how to measure a dip in starlight and share your observations with the researchers studying that planet. And the Unistellar Network Investigating TESS Exoplanets⁠(opens in a new window) coordinates volunteers around the world with a certain type of telescope to observe the same star, helping astronomers catch transits that can last longer than a single night.

Astronomy has a long history of people around the world following their curiosity and sharing what they find. Bond and Byrd are part of that tradition. Their searches are still open, but they turned a love of the night sky into leads that other astronomers can investigate. We want more people to have that opportunity, in astronomy and across science.

If you want to follow along with new findings, practical guidance, and perspectives from researchers using AI to advance science check out the OpenAI science blog⁠.

OpenAI董事长旗下Sierra官宣17.5亿美元融资，半年估值接近翻倍

OpenAI 董事长 Bret Taylor 创办的 AI 客服公司 Sierra 正式宣布新一轮 F 轮融资，融资规模达 17.5 亿美元，估值达到 300 亿美元。

这笔融资由 Greenoaks 和 Lightspeed 领投，红杉、Benchmark、GV 和 Tiger Global 等老股东继续加码。之前《The Information》爆料的融资规模约为 15 亿美元，最终公布的金额又提高了 2.5 亿美元。公司今年 5 月融资时估值为 158 亿美元，半年上涨约 90%。

Sierra 还披露了业务增长情况。公司目前已服务接近一半的《财富》美国前 50 大企业，包括摩根大通、汇丰银行、富国银行等金融巨头。

AI挖漏洞太快，补丁来不及打，OpenAI联合思科推出开源防御工具Shirudo

OpenAI 联合网络设备巨头思科（Cisco）开源安全工具 Shirudo。它能让 AI Agent 为存在漏洞的系统编写临时防护程序，无需等待正式补丁，也无需重启服务器。

如今 AI 发现和利用漏洞的速度越来越快，但企业测试、部署正式补丁仍可能需要数天甚至数周。直接关闭存在漏洞的功能，又可能导致正常业务中断。

Shirudo 由思科旗下的开源安全工具 Tetragon 重写而来，底层采用 Linux 的 eBPF 技术，可以在不重启系统的情况下改变其部分运行行为。过去，开发者主要通过预设的策略语言制定防御规则。如今，AI 可以直接编写代码，针对具体漏洞定制防护程序，并反复测试能否阻断攻击、是否影响正常业务。通过管理员审核和数字签名后，即可部署到运行中的系统。

OpenAI 希望未来在公开披露漏洞时，就能同步提供经过测试的临时防护程序，让企业在正式补丁部署前获得保护。

📱 小米三季度经调整净利同比下降 56.8%，汽车交付破 10 万辆

​小米集团发布 2026 年第三季度财报。集团经调整净利润为 48.84 亿元，同比大幅下降 56.8%，但仍略高于市场预期的 47.46 亿元；总营收达 1072.4 亿元，同比下滑 5.2%。分业务来看，“手机×AIoT”分部收入为 834 亿元，“新能源汽车及 AI 等创新业务”分部收入为 239 亿元。

​受存储芯片等核心元器件涨价及研发投入加码影响，集团整体盈利短期承压，三季度研发支出达 92.4 亿元，综合毛利率为 20.2%。核心手机业务当季出货量为 3070 万台，在主动收缩中低端机型后均价创下历史新高；汽车业务仍保持强劲增长势头，三季度小米共交付新车 100,975 辆。

items.body:
#Blog #AI #macOS #AD

🧑🏻‍💻 在快 AI 时代，我是怎么把 Mole 做成一款慢产品的？

🔗：Blog

这两个多月里 Mole 从 1.13 一路发到了 1.20，加了 AI 工具清理和系统数据清理，Windows 版也发了出来，不过回头看，花时间最多的反而不是写新功能，而是测软件、补发邮件、改图标和文案这些在工程师看来挺划不来的蠢事情。

为了让卸载更干净，本来想着测 100 个主流软件就够了，结果测完又想着再搞 100 个，一路加到了 853 款，电脑一下子变成了一个非常凌乱的桌面，好在 AI 还顺手自己写了安装、卸载、查残留的脚本，我基本就在旁边给它打打下手。原以为软件工程是规范的，测多了才发现很多残留怎么写规则都找不全，有些看着很规范的约定，可能只是当年某个程序员随手写的，只能装一个查一个。后面做 AI 清理也是这样，把 30 多款 AI 工具登录账号真实用了一遍，看到了不少离谱的事，有个命令行工具我只运行了一次，它没问我就自己装了新版本，还顺手改了 .zshrc，也有用户的 opencode.db 一个文件就涨到了 62 GB。

还有一件挺开心的事，国庆给 400 多单买了还没激活的用户一封封补发邮件，像发微信一样提醒一下，结果收到了很多国家的回信，有人买了两个，一个给自己，一个留给家人当圣诞礼物，Key 早就存进了密码管理器，让我感觉这个世界真美好。图标前前后后改了三轮才舒服，文案请 Gemini 当了一回很有耐心的语文老师，这些文章里也都聊了。

我反而觉得在代码没啥壁垒的年代，可以多做一点不可扩展的事情，只有自己亲手走一遍，才知道怎么让用户用的时候有那种秒懂、卧槽、变魔术的感觉。

频道：@NewlearnerChannel

百度文心5.5 Flash Preview正式开源：2800亿参数，支持百万Token

百度正式开源文心 ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview 模型权重，总参数 2800 亿，每个 Token 激活 140 亿参数，支持 100 万 Token 上下文。

11 月 5 日开源的 Base 底座采用百度自定义协议，限制欧盟、英国和韩国使用，相关业务年营收超过 5000 万美元还须单独获得商用授权。经过后训练的 Preview 版改用 Apache 2.0，允许全球开发者自由部署、微调和商用。

百度同时放出三种精度的权重。默认版将大部分专家参数压缩至 4-bit，模型文件约 166GB；FP8 版约 302GB，BF16 版约 600GB。默认版在后训练阶段就加入量化适配，可以直接按对应精度部署，不必另外量化。模型还内置 DSpark 推测解码模块，一次预测多个候选 Token，再由主模型批量验证，以提高生成速度。

模型现已在 Hugging Face 和 ModelScope 上架，提供 vLLM、SGLang 部署方案。

items.body:
腾讯混元翻译模型再升级：支持102种语言，联合王者荣耀优化游戏翻译

腾讯混元发布翻译模型 Hy-MT3，推出 1.8B、7B 和 30B-A3B 三个版本，支持语种从上一代的 38 种扩充至 102 种。

旗舰版总参数量为 300 亿，推理时仅激活 30 亿参数。官方评测显示，Hy-MT3 在通用翻译、真实场景翻译和指令遵循三项测试中，均超过非思考模式下的 Qwen3.8-Max、Kimi K3.1 Pro 和 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash。

其中，真实场景翻译拿到 91.30 分，超过思考模式下的 Gemini 4 Argon（90.30 分），距离同样开启思考模式的 GPT-6.1 Sol（92.50 分）仅差 1.2 分。在通用翻译测试中，Hy-MT3 的预估推理计算量还不到 Qwen3.8-Max 和 Kimi K3.1 Pro 的 1/30。不过，在专业知识密集的高难度翻译任务中，Hy-MT3 仍落后于头部通用大模型。

在 5000 条真实场景测试样本中，相比上一代旗舰版，新模型出现误译的样本比例从 56% 降至 31.8%，漏译或擅自增添内容的比例从 21.2% 降至 5.5%。甚至最小的 1.8B 版本，真实场景翻译得分也超过了上一代 30B 旗舰版。

腾讯还联合王者荣耀团队专门优化了游戏翻译。模型需要准确翻译技能描述、游戏术语，同时保留程序中的变量和富文本标签，避免译文导致客户端出错。在双方联合开展的人工评测中，Hy-MT3 的游戏术语错误率仅为 0.08%。

王者荣耀团队还宣布开源游戏翻译工具链，允许其他游戏厂商直接将模型接入研发流程。Hy-MT3 也已在腾讯 Hy 翻译 APP 和小程序上线。
